pos: n. (Nikolaus Selnecker, 1530–1592, Lutheran theologian, hymnwriter and organist, co-author of the Formula of Concord, driven repeatedly from Leipzig in the Crypto-Calvinist controversy)
etymology: German Selnecker, from Selneck; Nikolaus, from Greek Nikolaos, conqueror of the people.
biblical_def: Nikolaus Selnecker was a prodigy at the organ — court organist at twelve — who became a theologian without ceasing to be a musician. He studied under Melanchthon, taught at Jena and Leipzig, served as court preacher at Dresden, and with Andreae and Chemnitz was one of the authors of the Formula of Concord. His life was spent in the bitterest of the intra-Lutheran quarrels: twice expelled from Leipzig when the Crypto-Calvinist party held the Saxon court, twice restored, and finally recalled on his deathbed. What outlasted the controversies was his music. He wrote and set many hymns, among them Lass mich dein sein und bleiben, and edited collections that carried congregational singing through a generation of strife. Col 3:16 is the warrant for the whole of it: “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.” Eph 5:19 repeats it, and 2Ch 20:21 is the striking case of how “he appointed singers unto the LORD” and sent out before an army.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hymn as a song or ode in honor of God, and among pagans, in honor of some deity; and psalmody as the art or practice of singing sacred songs.
webster_full: HYMN, n. A song or ode in honor of God, and among pagans, in honor of some deity.
HYMN, v.t. To praise in song; to worship or extol by singing hymns.
PSAL'MODY, n. The act, practice or art of singing sacred songs.
scriptures: Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
Psa 98:1
A Psalm. O sing unto the LORD a new song; for he hath done marvellous things: his right hand, and his holy arm, hath gotten him the victory.

And when he had consulted with the people, he appointed singers unto the LORD, and that should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army, and to say, Praise the LORD; for his mercy endureth for ever.
corruption_summary: Selnecker was expelled twice for his doctrine and remembered for his hymns, which is how a church actually carries what it believes.
corruption_paragraphs: Col 3:16 joins two things the modern church tends to separate: the word of Christ dwelling richly, and the singing. Singing is there a means of teaching and admonishing, which makes the content of a hymn a doctrinal matter and not a question of taste. Selnecker understood this and wrote accordingly, and his hymns survived the controversies that consumed his career because a congregation remembers what it sings. A church that treats its music as mood-setting has surrendered one of the two instruments the verse names.

The Reformed caution concerns what may be sung and on whose authority. The regulative principle requires warrant for the elements of worship, and Col 3:16 and Eph 5:19 together give psalms, hymns and spiritual songs — which the exclusive-psalmody position reads as three descriptions of the Psalter and others read more broadly. The dictionary does not settle that question here; it insists on the prior one, that singing is commanded, is congregational, is addressed to the Lord, and must teach the truth. 2Ch 20:21 shows how seriously God has taken appointed singers.

pos: n. (Matthew Zell, 1477–1548, the first evangelical preacher of Strasbourg and its most pastoral, who with his wife Katharina sheltered refugees of every party)
etymology: German Zell, from a cell or hermitage, a place-name surname; Matthäus, the Greek form of Matthew.
biblical_def: Matthew Zell began preaching the gospel in Strasbourg cathedral in 1521 and was so plainly loved by the townspeople that when the bishop locked the pulpit the carpenters' guild built him a portable one. He married Katharina Schütz in 1523, among the first clergy in the city to do so, and their house became a hostel: Zell and his wife took in Peasants' War refugees, exiled Swiss, and Anabaptists whom the magistrates were expelling, arguing that men in error were to be persuaded rather than drowned. He was no great theologian and did not pretend to be — Bucer and Capito did the city's doctrinal work — and he was the one whose funeral filled the streets. Mat 9:36 is the temper of his ministry: Christ “was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.” Rom 12:13 commands the practice, “given to hospitality,” and Gal 6:1 the manner with the erring, to “restore such an one in the spirit of meekness.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines compassion as a suffering with another; painful sympathy; and meekness as softness of temper; mildness; gentleness; forbearance under injuries and provocations.
webster_full: COMPAS'SION, n. A suffering with another; painful sympathy; a sensation of sorrow excited by the distress or misfortunes of another; pity; commiseration.
MEEK'NESS, n. Softness of temper; mildness; gentleness; forbearance under injuries and provocations.
2. In an evangelical sense, humility; resignation; submission to the divine will.
scriptures: Mat 9:36
But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.
Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality.
Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
Jud 1:22
And of some have compassion, making a difference:
corruption_summary: Zell sheltered men his city was drowning, and a Reformation that could not tell error from criminality is the thing he was arguing against.
corruption_paragraphs: The Protestant cities executed Anabaptists, and Strasbourg was unusually restrained partly because of Zell and his wife. The doctrine at issue was real — this dictionary holds believer's baptism and rejects the Münster errors, the oath-refusal and the celestial-flesh Christology alike — and the question Zell pressed was what a church may do to a man who is wrong. Gal 6:1 gives the answer for a brother overtaken in a fault: restore him in meekness. Jud 1:22 adds a word of discrimination, “of some have compassion, making a difference,” which is not indifference but judgment exercised case by case rather than by execution.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is pastoral compassion as a duty of office rather than a temperament. Mat 9:36 attributes it to Christ in the presence of crowds who had teachers and no shepherd, and the ministry is to be shaped by that sight. A church may hold its confession exactly and still fail here, and Zell is the standing example of a man of modest doctrinal gifts whose house did what the city's theologians argued about.
roots_summary: Greek splagchnizomai (G4697), to be moved in the inward parts; philoxenia (G5381), hospitality; katartizo (G2675), to restore.

“given to hospitality” (Rom 12:13) — commanded, and practised in his house.
“restore such an one in the spirit of meekness” (Gal 6:1) — the manner with the erring.

pos: n. (Lambert Daneau, c. 1530–1595, French Reformed pastor and theologian, Beza's colleague at Geneva and professor at Leiden, author of the first Reformed system of Christian ethics)
biblical_def: Lambert Daneau was converted by the death of Anne du Bourg, a councillor burned at Paris in 1559, studied under Calvin and Beza, pastored in France through the wars, and taught at Geneva and then as the first professor of theology at Leiden. His Ethices Christianae of 1577 is the first full Reformed system of Christian ethics, and its method is the lasting contribution: it organizes the moral life under the Decalogue, treats the law as the believer's rule and not his righteousness, and derives duties from Scripture rather than from Aristotle's virtues. Mic 6:8 is its governing question — “what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” Tit 2:12 gives grace itself as the teacher, “Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world.” Rom 12:2 forbids conformity to the world, and Psa 119:11 names the means: “Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ethics as the doctrine of morals; a system of moral principles; the science of moral philosophy, which teaches men their duty and the reasons of it.
webster_full: ETH'ICS, n. The doctrine of morals; a system of moral principles; a system of rules for regulating the actions and manners of men in society.
ETH'ICAL, a. Relating to morals or manners; treating of morality; delivering precepts of morality.
MORAL'ITY, n. The doctrine or system of moral duties, or the duties of men in their social character.
scriptures: Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
Tit 2:12
Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world;
Rom 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.
corruption_summary: Daneau built Christian ethics on the Decalogue under grace, which is the only arrangement that is neither legalism nor the loss of the law.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors stand on either side of Daneau's method. The first is legalism, which makes obedience the ground of acceptance; the Reformed answer is that the believer is justified by faith alone and the law is thereafter his rule, not his righteousness. The second is antinomianism, which concludes from justification that the law has no further claim; Tit 2:12 forecloses it by making grace itself the teacher of sober and righteous living. Daneau's arrangement — the Decalogue as the structure of Christian duty, within a covenant of grace — is the one the Heidelberg Catechism and the Westminster Larger follow, and it is the standing Reformed shape of ethics.

The nearer corruption is the modern substitution of principles for commandments. Christian ethics is now commonly taught as the application of broad values — love, justice, flourishing — to cases, which sounds generous and in practice lets the culture supply the content of each term. Mic 6:8 is often quoted in that service, with the third clause quietly dropped; the verse requires walking humbly with God, which anchors justice and mercy to His revealed will. The recovery is Daneau's: ten commandments, expounded, applied, and preached to the justified.
roots_summary: Greek eusebeia, godliness; suschematizo (G4964), to conform to a pattern; Hebrew tsana (H6800), to be humble.
roots_lines: Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, justice; Micah 6:8.
Hebrew tsana (H6800) — to be lowly, to walk humbly; Micah 6:8.

“denying ungodliness and worldly lusts” (Tit 2:12) — grace as the teacher.

pos: n. (the Colloquy of Regensburg, 1541, the imperial conference at which Contarini, Melanchthon and Bucer agreed an article of double justification that both Rome and the Reformers rejected)
etymology: Latin colloquium, a speaking together; Regensburg on the Danube, called Ratisbon in older English books.
biblical_def: The Colloquy of Regensburg was Charles V's most serious attempt at reunion. He needed a united empire against the Turk, and in 1541 he brought the parties together on a secret draft — the Regensburg Book — with Contarini as papal legate, Gropper and Eck for Rome, Melanchthon and Bucer for the Protestants. On most heads they failed. On justification they produced Article Five, which said that the believer is accepted on account of the imputed righteousness of Christ and also receives an inherent righteousness, and for a few weeks it looked like agreement. Then Rome repudiated it and so did Luther and Calvin, who saw that a ground which is partly inherent is not grace. The colloquy is the classic case of the compromise that satisfies nobody because the question admits no middle. 1Ki 18:21 is Elijah's word to a people who wanted both — “How long halt ye between two opinions?” — and Jas 1:8, “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colloquy as conversation; mutual discourse of two or more; a dialogue; and a conference as a meeting for consultation or discussion.
webster_full: COL'LOQUY, n. Conversation; mutual discourse of two or more; a dialogue.
CON'FERENCE, n. A meeting of several persons for consultation, or for the discussion of some subject.
COM'PROMISE, n. A mutual promise or contract of two parties in controversy, to refer their differences to the decision of arbitrators.
scriptures: And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word.
Jas 1:8
A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.
Rev 3:16
So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
Mat 6:24
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
corruption_summary: Regensburg shows that on justification there is no third position, only a form of words that each side reads its own way.
corruption_paragraphs: Article Five was skilfully drafted and that was its defect: it could be signed by men who meant opposite things. Rome read the inherent righteousness as the formal cause of justification; the Protestants read the imputed righteousness as the sole ground with sanctification following. A formula that both can sign has not resolved the question, it has postponed it, and the postponement was exposed within weeks. Mat 6:24 states the structural impossibility in another sphere: a man cannot finally serve two masters, and a doctrine cannot finally rest on two grounds.

The modern descendant is the ecumenical statement that declares the historic condemnations inapplicable while leaving the defining canons in force, and it fails in the same way and for the same reason. Rev 3:16 is addressed to a church that is “neither cold nor hot,” and the warning is not against courtesy but against a settled indifference to the truth of the matter. Real agreement is possible and is reached the way the Formula of Concord reached it — by stating the question, naming the errors, and defining the answer at length.
roots_summary: Hebrew pacach (H6452), to limp, to halt; Greek dipsuchos (G1374), double-souled; chliaros (G5513), lukewarm.
roots_lines: Hebrew pacach (H6452) — to limp, to halt between; 1 Kings 18:21.
Greek dipsuchos (G1374) — double-minded, two-souled; James 1:8.

Greek chliaros (G5513) — lukewarm, tepid; Revelation 3:16.

“A double minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jas 1:8) — a doctrine on two grounds.
“No man can serve two masters” (Mat 6:24) — the structural impossibility.

pos: n. (the Peace of Augsburg, 1555, the imperial settlement that legalized Lutheranism on the principle cuius regio, eius religio — whose the realm, his the religion — and excluded the Reformed)
etymology: Latin pax, peace; Augsburg in Swabia, where the Diet sat. The tag cuius regio, eius religio was coined later to describe its principle.
biblical_def: The Peace of Augsburg ended twenty-five years of religious war in the Empire by a device: each prince would determine the religion of his own territory, Lutheran or Catholic, and subjects who could not conform were to be permitted to emigrate. It gave the Lutheran churches legal standing for the first time and bought Germany half a century of quiet. It also established the principle that a man's confession follows his ruler's, which is not peace but a postponement, and it recognized only two religions — the Reformed were left outside, a grievance that helped produce the Thirty Years War. Mat 22:21 marks the boundary the settlement crossed: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.” Faith is not Caesar's to assign. Dan 3:18 is the answer of men whose ruler had chosen for them: “be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods.” 1Pe 2:17 keeps the honour due: “Fear God. Honour the king.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines toleration as the allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, when contrary to or different from those of the established church.
webster_full: TOLERA'TION, n. The act of tolerating; the allowance of that which is not wholly approved.
2. Allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, when contrary to or different from those of the established church or belief.
CON'SCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge, or judgment of right and wrong.
scriptures: They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
Dan 3:18
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.
So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God.
corruption_summary: Cuius regio, eius religio made a prince the arbiter of his subjects' souls, which is the error both Rome and the Protestant establishments shared.
corruption_paragraphs: The settlement treated religion as an attribute of territory. That is a category error with eternal consequences, because Rom 14:12 says “every one of us shall give account of himself to God” — himself, not his prince — and a man cannot delegate that account to a Diet. The device worked politically and was wrong in principle, and its logic is what put Lutherans out of Catholic lands and Reformed out of both. Dan 3:18 is the standing refusal, spoken by three men to the most powerful ruler of their world, with the consequences fully in view.

The 1689 Confession draws the line the sixteenth century could not: the civil magistrate has no authority over the faith and worship of the saints, and Christ alone is Lord of the conscience. That is not a plea for indifference — the same Confession binds the church to its doctrine strictly — but for the right instrument. Faith is produced by the Word and the Spirit, not by a territorial decree, and 1Pe 2:17 shows how to live under a ruler whose religion is not yours: fear God first, and honour the king genuinely.

“we will not serve thy gods” (Dan 3:18) — the answer to a ruler who chooses for you.
“every one of us shall give account of himself to God” (Rom 14:12) — himself, not his prince.

pos: n. (the Augsburg Interim, 1548, the settlement Charles V imposed on the defeated Protestants after the Schmalkaldic War, which provoked the Adiaphorist controversy)
etymology: Latin interim, in the meantime — so called because it was to hold until a general council should decide.
biblical_def: The Augsburg Interim was victory terms. Having beaten the Schmalkaldic League, Charles V imposed a settlement that restored Roman doctrine and ceremony almost entire, conceding only clerical marriage and the cup to the laity, and required the Protestant territories to accept it until a council should rule. The crisis it produced was not about its doctrine, which the Lutherans rejected outright, but about its ceremonies. Melanchthon and the Wittenberg party, under pressure from Elector Maurice, accepted a modified version — the Leipzig Interim — on the ground that vestments, fasts and holy days are adiaphora, things indifferent, which may be conceded to keep the churches open. Flacius and the strict party answered that nothing is indifferent when it is demanded as a token of submission. Gal 2:3 is the apostolic precedent on their side: “neither Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised.” Circumcision was indifferent, and Paul refused it when it was exacted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines indifferent as neither good nor bad; having no influence or preponderating weight; and an interim as the mean time; the intervening time.
webster_full: IN'TERIM, n. The mean time; time intervening.
INDIF'FERENT, a. Neutral; not favoring one party or the other; impartial.
4. Neither good nor bad; of a middle state or quality; as, in things indifferent.
scriptures: Gal 2:3
But neither Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised:
But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak.
And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin.
Col 2:20
Wherefore if ye be dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, are ye subject to ordinances,
corruption_summary: A thing indifferent stops being indifferent the moment it is demanded as the price of submission, and that is the whole Adiaphorist controversy.
corruption_paragraphs: The Wittenberg argument was not foolish: a vestment is a vestment, and keeping pulpits open is a real good. The strict party saw further. When a ceremony is exacted precisely as an acknowledgment of a false authority, conceding it concedes the authority, and the people watching learn that the church will yield. Paul grasped this exactly. He circumcised Timothy freely for the sake of the Jews and flatly refused to circumcise Titus when the false brethren demanded it, because by then the rite had become a test of the gospel. Gal 2:3 is the case, and the principle generalizes: in a time of confession, indifferent things cease to be indifferent.

The balancing truth is that liberty is real and may be limited for others' sake, which is the error of making every scruple a confession. 1Co 8:9 warns against liberty becoming “a stumblingblock to them that are weak,” and Rom 14:23 binds a man to act from faith. Col 2:20 asks why those dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world are “subject to ordinances.” The recovery is the distinction: concede freely in peace for love's sake, concede nothing under compulsion that is demanded as a mark of surrender.
roots_summary: Greek anagkazo (G315), to compel; proskomma (G4348), a stumblingblock; dogmatizo (G1379), to be subject to ordinances.

Greek proskomma (G4348) — a stumblingblock; 1 Corinthians 8:9.
Greek exousia (G1849) — liberty, right; 1 Corinthians 8:9.
Greek diakrino (G1252) — to doubt, to waver; Romans 14:23.
Greek dogmatizo (G1379) — to be subject to decrees; Colossians 2:20.
usage: “neither Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised” (Gal 2:3) — an indifferent thing refused when exacted.
“take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock” (1Co 8:9) — the balancing truth.
“why, as though living in the world, are ye subject to ordinances” (Col 2:20) — the question put to the Leipzig concession.

pos: n. (the Smalcald Articles, 1537, Luther's own confession drawn up for a general council, the sharpest statement of the chief article and of the case against the papacy)
etymology: From Schmalkalden in Thuringia, where the Protestant league met; article from Latin articulus, a joint, a clause.
biblical_def: The Smalcald Articles were written by Luther in the winter of 1536 at the Elector's request, in case the general council then summoned to Mantua should actually sit and the Protestants be required to state their faith. He was ill and expected to die, and the document has the directness of a last testament. It divides into three parts: the articles not in dispute, on the Trinity and the person of Christ; the articles that admit no yielding, on the chief article of justification, the mass, the invocation of saints, monasteries and the papacy; and the articles for discussion with learned men. The second part is the heart. “Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom 3:24) is his chief article, with Rom 4:25, that Christ “was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification,” and Act 10:43, that “whosoever believeth in him shall receive remission of sins.” Isa 43:25 is God speaking for Himself: “I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession of faith as a summary of the articles of Christian faith, received and professed by a church; and justification as an act of free grace.
webster_full: CONFES'SION, n. A profession of belief; a creed.
2. In church history, a formulary of articles of faith; as the Augsburg confession.
JUSTIFICA'TION, n. In theology, remission of sin and absolution from guilt and punishment; or an act of free grace.
scriptures: Rom 3:24
Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:
Rom 4:25
Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.
To him give all the prophets witness, that through his name whosoever believeth in him shall receive remission of sins.
I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.
corruption_summary: Luther wrote the Smalcald Articles expecting to die, and what he refused to yield is the shortest list of what the Reformation was for.
corruption_paragraphs: The structure of the document is its argument. Luther puts the Trinity and the incarnation among the articles not in dispute, which is a confession of catholic orthodoxy against the charge of novelty; he then names what cannot be conceded, and the first of these is justification. He calls it the chief article and says that on it everything depends, so that if it stands the church stands. Rom 3:24 gives the three words the article turns on — justified, freely, by grace — and Rom 4:25 attaches it to the resurrection, which is why a merely exemplary Christ cannot supply it.

The articles against the papacy are the sharpest Luther ever published and are sometimes dismissed as the invective of a sick and angry man. The substance is not invective: he argues that the claim to rule the church by divine right over Scripture is what makes every other error irreformable, since a wrong that no text may correct will not be corrected. Isa 43:25 is the verse that most offends the whole apparatus of merit and satisfaction, because God blots out transgressions “for mine own sake” — not for a treasury's, not for a saint's, and not for the sinner's own.
roots_summary: Greek dorean (G1432), freely, without cost; apolutrosis (G629), redemption; Hebrew machah (H4229), to blot out.
roots_lines: Greek dorean (G1432) — freely, as a gift; Romans 3:24.
Greek apolutrosis (G629) — redemption, release by ransom; Romans 3:24.
Greek paradidomi (G3860) — to deliver up; Romans 4:25.
Greek aphesis (G859) — remission, release; Acts 10:43.
Hebrew machah (H4229) — to wipe out, to blot out; Isaiah 43:25.
usage: “Being justified freely by his grace” (Rom 3:24) — the chief article.
“was raised again for our justification” (Rom 4:25) — attached to the resurrection.
“I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake” (Isa 43:25) — against every treasury of merit.

pos: n. (the Schmalkaldic League, 1531–1547, the defensive alliance of Lutheran princes and cities against Charles V, destroyed at Mühlberg)
etymology: From Schmalkalden in Thuringia, where the league was formed; league from Old French ligue, from Latin ligare, to bind.
biblical_def: The Schmalkaldic League was formed in 1531 by the Lutheran princes and free cities, headed by Philip of Hesse and John Frederick of Saxony, to defend themselves against an emperor sworn to restore the old religion by force. Its existence raised a question the Reformers had to answer rather than avoid: may a Christian prince take arms against his lawful overlord for religion? Luther, who had refused the idea for years, was persuaded by the jurists' argument that the emperor is bound by imperial law and that a prince resisting a lawless emperor resists not the office but the breach of it — the seed of the Protestant resistance theory that Beza, the Huguenots and the Covenanters would develop. The league held the empire in check for sixteen years, then lost everything in a single campaign; John Frederick and Philip were captured at Mühlberg in 1547 and the Augsburg Interim followed. Psa 20:7 is the verse the defeat preached: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.” Pro 21:31 says “safety is of the LORD.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a league as an alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defense; and resistance as the act of resisting; opposition.
webster_full: LEAGUE, n. An alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defense.
LEAGUE, v.i. To unite, as princes or states, in a contract of amity for mutual aid or defense.
RESIST'ANCE, n. The act of resisting; opposition; the quality of not yielding to force or external impression.
scriptures: Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD.
Neh 4:14

And I looked, and rose up, and said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, Be not ye afraid of them: remember the Lord, which is great and terrible, and fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses.
Be of good courage, and let us play the men for our people, and for the cities of our God: and the LORD do that which seemeth him good.
corruption_summary: The league asked whether a prince may resist an emperor for religion, and the answer the jurists gave shaped two centuries of Protestant politics.
corruption_paragraphs: Luther's early position was non-resistance: the magistrate is ordained of God and a subject suffers rather than rebels. What changed his mind was not expedience but a distinction — that the empire was a constitutional order in which the princes were themselves magistrates with sworn duties, so that resisting an emperor who broke the law was the lesser magistrate defending the order, not a private man taking the sword. Neh 4:14 is the text such men reached for: “fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses.” The doctrine is a serious one, worked out further by Beza and the Huguenot writers, and it is not a licence for private insurrection.

The defeat is the other half of the lesson, and the league's own members drew it. Sixteen years of alliance-building, subsidies and marriages ended in one afternoon at Mühlberg, and the churches were then saved not by arms but by the fact that men went on preaching and refusing under the Interim. Psa 20:7 does not forbid the horse; it forbids trusting it. 2Sa 10:12 holds the balance for a lawful war: “let us play the men for our people, and for the cities of our God: and the LORD do that which seemeth him good.”

pos: n. (the Hampton Court Conference, January 1604, at which James I heard the Puritan petitioners, refused nearly all their requests, and authorized a new translation of the Bible)
etymology: Hampton Court Palace on the Thames; conference from Latin conferre, to bring together.
biblical_def: The Hampton Court Conference was convened after the Millenary Petition, in which something like a thousand ministers asked the new king for reform of the English church: an end to pluralism and non-residence, a learned preaching ministry, relief from the surplice and the ring in marriage and the sign of the cross in baptism, and a stricter sabbath. James heard them for three days and granted almost nothing; when Reynolds used the word presbytery the king lost his temper, and the conference ended with the famous threat of “no bishop, no king.” Hundreds of ministers were deprived in the following years. One request was granted, almost in passing, because the king happened to dislike the Geneva Bible's notes: a new translation, which became the Authorized Version of 1611. Isa 55:11 is the providence of it — “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” — and Pro 19:21, “There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a conference as a meeting of several persons for consultation, or for the discussion of some subject; and a petition as a request; a prayer.
webster_full: CON'FERENCE, n. A meeting of several persons for consultation, or for the discussion of some subject.
2. A meeting for religious exercises.
PETI'TION, n. In a general sense, a request, supplication or prayer; a formal request or supplication.
scriptures: So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it.
There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand.
But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
Act 4:28
For to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done.
corruption_summary: A king refused the Puritans almost everything and granted them a Bible, and four hundred years later the Bible is what remains.
corruption_paragraphs: Hampton Court is the clearest case in English history of Gen 50:20 working in a church's affairs: “ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.” James intended to consolidate episcopal government and clip the Puritans, and he largely succeeded; the ministers went away with their grievances intact, and the deprivations that followed drove some of them to Holland and thence to Plymouth. What the conference produced that nobody present reckoned the chief business was the translation that formed English-speaking Christianity for four centuries. Pro 19:21 is the structure of the event, not a consolation for it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the distinction between what a court grants and what God accomplishes. Act 4:28 describes rulers doing “whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done” — said of the crucifixion, the worst act in history and the appointed means of salvation. A church denied its reforms by an unsympathetic authority is not therefore outside God's purpose, and the Puritans who went home empty-handed in 1604 were handed, without knowing it, the instrument of their own tradition's greatest influence.

pos: n. (the Acts of Supremacy, 1534 and 1559, which made the English sovereign Supreme Head and then Supreme Governor of the Church of England)
etymology: Latin supremus, highest; the 1534 act styled the king Supreme Head, the 1559 act styled Elizabeth Supreme Governor, a deliberate softening.
biblical_def: The Act of Supremacy of 1534 declared Henry VIII “the only supreme head in earth of the Church of England” and annexed to the crown the authority to visit, reform and correct all errors and heresies. Refusal to swear to it cost Thomas More and John Fisher their heads. Repealed under Mary, it was re-enacted in 1559 with the title changed to Supreme Governor, partly to meet the objection that no human being can be head of Christ's church. The objection is the right one, and Scripture states it without qualification: “he is the head of the body, the church” (Col 1:18), and God “gave him to be the head over all things to the church” (Eph 1:22). The headship is Christ's by gift of the Father and is not transferable to a pope or a prince. Mat 23:10 forbids the title in any hand: “Neither be ye called masters: for one is your Master, even Christ.” 1Pe 5:4 names Him “the chief Shepherd,” under whom the elders of each congregation are undershepherds and nothing more.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines supremacy as the state of being supreme or in the highest station of power; highest authority or power; and headship as authority; chief place.
webster_full: SUPREM'ACY, n. State of being supreme, or in the highest station of power; highest authority or power.
The articles of the church of England assert the supremacy of the king in ecclesiastical as well as civil affairs.
HEAD'SHIP, n. Authority; chief place.
scriptures: Col 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
Eph 1:22
And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church,
Neither be ye called masters: for one is your Master, even Christ.
And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.
corruption_summary: England exchanged one usurper of Christ's headship for another and called it a reformation of the church's government.
corruption_paragraphs: The error in the Act is the same error Rome had made, relocated. The papal claim and the royal claim are both claims to a headship Scripture assigns exclusively to Christ, and the 1559 softening from Head to Governor conceded the point in words while keeping the substance: the crown appointed bishops, licensed preaching, authorized the liturgy and judged ecclesiastical causes. Col 1:18 and Eph 1:22 do not leave an office vacant for a sovereign to fill. This is why the Puritans and after them the Separatists and the Baptists could not rest in the Elizabethan settlement: the question was not ceremonies but who governs the church.

The positive doctrine is congregational and is the 1689 Confession's: Christ is the only head, He rules by His Word and Spirit, and He has appointed in each congregation elders and deacons — elders plural, chosen by the church, holding no civil power and answerable to the chief Shepherd. 1Pe 5:4 is the whole structure in a phrase, since a chief Shepherd implies undershepherds and excludes a vicar. Mat 23:10 removes the title from every human claimant, prince or pontiff, and leaves it where it belongs.
